articles.title: Indonesia’s Mama Aleta: Don’t wait for permission to protect Mother Nature
articles.summary: Two decades after Mollo women resisted marble mining in Indonesia, the climate crisis brings new urgency to their struggle for nature, Indigenous rights and collective action.
articles.content:
We Mollo women stood up against mining companies to protect Mother Nature in Timor Island, eastern Indonesia. We did this because we believe that Mother Earth is not just a dead rock and soil, but a living body. The land is our flesh (Afu fani on nesa), the water is our blood (Oel fani on na), the rock is our bones (Fatu fani on nuif), and the forest is our hair and lungs (Nasi fani on nafua).

If you hurt the Earth, you hurt our bodies.

Being on the frontlines, I feel an urgency, more than ever before, to stand up against those hurting our Earth. For generations, Mollo people have read the skies and the winds to determine the harvest. But climate change has made predictions more difficult. In Timor, sudden excessive rains and prolonged dry seasons have confused people about when to plant their crops over the past three years. They are worried this will lead to a food crisis.

Nowadays, they all talk about solving issues such as stunting in children. But only in terms of food policy or programmes. True health comes from fertile soil. If you destroy our natural resources, rob Indigenous lands and turn them into large-pit mines or agricultural plantations, how are you supposed to grow these nutrients? I think stunting is not just about a lack of nutrition, but about how damaged the environment is. You cannot heal the people while continuing to poison the land that sustains them.

We do not reject development. We still need it. But not development that destroys nature and strips away the rights of Indigenous peoples. They build hotels, allow mining extraction, while Indigenous peoples guard water resources and protect the ecology. We, the people and the state, must re-evaluate how we consider this kind of development.

People often look back at our movement in Mollo, where Indigenous women sat at the marble quarries for months, peacefully weaving cloth until the mining operations were forced to shut. Our struggle succeeded because women and men together united, sharing the view that ecological destruction means the death of our culture, health and future. I recall someone saying firmly: “We are not thieves; we are fighting for our rights.”

When I look at today — climate crisis, food crisis, drought — I feel upset. I feel exhausted, tired and fed up. It’s like this country is deaf. It is frustrating that the state does not consider human lives, but focuses instead on money, or one-sided interests. Not development for us, but often simply personal business transactions that sacrifice the needs of people.

But I never think about giving up. If we let things be, we are the ones who will suffer. They will destroy things and leave, because they have a secure life. Us? This is where we live. So we need to fight back and find new strategies to hold our ground and fight to save our Earth.

When you talk about nature, you are talking about mothers. Women have many strategies. They are capable, smart and resilient. Importantly, they refuse to back down and always find a way. When a woman says she is fighting for something deeply important, God and our ancestors shield and support her in breaking free from all oppression. But for these strengths to emerge, women have to step up.

Being a female leader is about how to find new strategies to bring people together so they can collectively take action. I always think that is what real leadership is. Often, as women, we fall for the assumption that becoming a leader must mean waiting for people to choose us. This is wrong. We don’t have to join a political party or be voted in to call ourselves leaders. If you can bring together two or three or 10 people to do work that is in the public interest — that protects Mother Earth — that is leadership, right there.

To the younger generation, don’t waste your time doing unimportant things which don’t protect Earth or save future generations. Learn about nature, which provides our economy, food, health and education. The future lies within the natural wealth that is available to us. For governments, my hope is that they reflect on their actions regarding the destruction of natural resources. There must be real, thorough assessments, and they must listen to the voices of the people. Without the people, the state wouldn’t even exist.

As Dialogue Earth celebrates 20 years of giving voice to environmental issues, my message to grassroots activists across Southeast Asia and the world remains simple: never wait for permission to defend your home. Stand united, listen to the land, and remember that when you protect nature, you are protecting your own body and the generations that are yet to come.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the inspiring and impactful grassroots environmental activism led by Indigenous Mollo women in Indonesia, who successfully resisted destructive mining practices and continue to advocate for protecting nature and Indigenous rights amid climate and food crises. It emphasizes collective action, Indigenous leadership, and the deep connection between environmental health and human well-being, offering a hopeful and meaningful narrative with broad societal relevance.
articles.personality_title: Indigenous Mollo women lead fight to protect nature and community in Indonesia
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For over 20 years, Indigenous Mollo women on Timor Island in eastern Indonesia have stood against mining companies that threaten their land. They see the Earth as a living body, with the land, water, rocks, and forest all connected to their own health and culture.

**What happened** – Two decades ago, Mollo women peacefully resisted marble mining by sitting at quarries and weaving cloth until operations stopped. Today, they continue to fight against environmental harm caused by mining, plantations, and climate change that disrupts farming and causes food worries.

**Impact** – Their movement shows how protecting nature is linked to protecting people’s health and culture. Mollo women highlight that damaged soil leads to poor nutrition and stunting in children. Their leadership proves that local communities can unite to defend their land and rights, even when governments focus on money or business interests.

**What's next step** – The women encourage others, especially young people, to learn about nature and take action without waiting for permission. They call on governments to listen to Indigenous voices and carefully assess the impact of development on natural resources.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Mollo women’s long-standing activism teaches that caring for the Earth is essential to protecting communities and future generations.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les femmes Mollo protègent la nature et leur communauté en Indonésie
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis plus de 20 ans, les femmes autochtones Mollo de l’île de Timor, dans l’est de l’Indonésie, s’opposent aux compagnies minières qui menacent leur terre. Elles considèrent la Terre comme un corps vivant, où la terre, l’eau, les roches et la forêt sont liés à leur santé et culture.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Il y a deux décennies, les femmes Mollo ont résisté pacifiquement à l’extraction de marbre en s’asseyant dans les carrières et en tissant des tissus jusqu’à l’arrêt des opérations. Aujourd’hui, elles continuent de lutter contre les dégâts causés par les mines, les plantations et le changement climatique qui perturbe l’agriculture et inquiète pour la nourriture.

**Impact** – Leur mouvement montre que protéger la nature revient à protéger la santé et la culture des gens. Les femmes Mollo soulignent que la terre abîmée cause une mauvaise nutrition et un retard de croissance chez les enfants. Leur leadership prouve que les communautés locales peuvent s’unir pour défendre leurs terres et droits, même si les gouvernements privilégient l’argent ou les affaires.

**Prochaine étape** – Ces femmes encouragent les autres, surtout les jeunes, à apprendre la nature et agir sans attendre une permission. Elles appellent les gouvernements à écouter les voix autochtones et à évaluer sérieusement l’impact du développement sur les ressources naturelles.

**Une phrase clé** – L’activisme des femmes Mollo montre que prendre soin de la Terre est essentiel pour protéger les communautés et les générations futures.
articles.personality_title_es: Mujeres indígenas Mollo lideran la defensa de la naturaleza y su comunidad en Indonesia
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante más de 20 años, las mujeres indígenas Mollo en la isla de Timor, al este de Indonesia, se han opuesto a las empresas mineras que amenazan sus tierras. Ven la Tierra como un cuerpo vivo, donde la tierra, el agua, las rocas y el bosque están conectados con su salud y cultura.

**Qué pasó** – Hace dos décadas, las mujeres Mollo resistieron pacíficamente la minería de mármol sentándose en las canteras y tejiendo telas hasta que las operaciones se detuvieron. Hoy continúan luchando contra el daño ambiental causado por la minería, las plantaciones y el cambio climático que afecta la agricultura y genera preocupación por la comida.

**Impacto** – Su movimiento demuestra cómo proteger la naturaleza está ligado a proteger la salud y cultura de las personas. Las mujeres Mollo resaltan que el suelo dañado provoca mala nutrición y retraso en el crecimiento de los niños. Su liderazgo muestra que las comunidades locales pueden unirse para defender sus tierras y derechos, incluso cuando los gobiernos priorizan el dinero o los intereses comerciales.

**Próximo paso** – Las mujeres animan a otros, especialmente a los jóvenes, a aprender sobre la naturaleza y actuar sin esperar permiso. Piden a los gobiernos que escuchen las voces indígenas y evalúen cuidadosamente el impacto del desarrollo en los recursos naturales.

**Una frase clave** – El activismo de las mujeres Mollo enseña que cuidar la Tierra es esencial para proteger a las comunidades y a las futuras generaciones.

articles.title: The haunting loveliness of boglands: Books in brief
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03885-4Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.
articles.content:
Boglands

Merritt R. Turetsky Profile (2026)

Boglands are formed by waterlogged conditions and a lack of oxygen that slows down plant decomposition, causing organic matter to accumulate as a thick layer of peat. Peatlands occupy only 3% of the planet’s land area, but store about 30% of soil carbon. “In this liminal space, where land is water and water is land,” writes ecologist Merritt Turetsky, “a strange and haunting loveliness reveals itself.” This is not obvious to most people, who often laugh when told that she studies bogs. Such sceptics will be won over by her fascinating book.

The Carbon Wave

Leah C. Stokes MIT Press (2026)

At university, environmentalist Leah Stokes was stirred by the 2006 documentary An Inconvenient Truth, which argued that each of us is responsible for reducing global warming. Only later, as an associate professor in California, did she realize that the chief culprit is fossil-fuel infrastructure. In 2022, Stokes had a major role in pushing the US government to pass landmark legislation, the Inflation Reduction Act, with more than US$400 billion in climate investments. Her absorbing book unpacks “the blow-by-blows of how this climate law was made”.

The Power To Destroy

James K. Galbraith Univ. Chicago Press (2026)

Veteran economist James Galbraith begins his striking attack on mainstream economics in the United States by declaring that his academic discipline has long been a “fraud”. For decades, economists have embraced the idea that “power over money should be kept far from democratic politics”. And yet, oligarchs from finance, technology, pharmaceuticals and several other fields now hold political power. Economists, he argues, continue to deploy outdated tools from a century ago, which are weakening democracy.

Oxford Physics and the Modern World

Timothy M. M. Baker World Scientific (2026)
articles.reasoning: The article highlights important books focusing on environmental science and climate action, including the critical role of peatlands in carbon storage and significant climate legislation in the US. These topics have broad societal and environmental impact, providing inspiring insights into conservation and climate policy.
articles.personality_title: New books reveal how nature and policy shape our future
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists and writers are exploring important topics like the environment, climate change, and economics through new books published in 2026. These books help us understand how nature works and how laws and ideas affect our world.

**What happened** – Five notable books were reviewed, each offering unique insights. Merritt Turetsky’s book explains how boglands, special wet areas called peatlands, store lots of carbon and help fight climate change. Leah Stokes shares how she helped pass a major US law investing over $400 billion to reduce global warming. James Galbraith challenges old economic ideas and shows how money and power affect politics today. Another book by Timothy Baker looks at how physics connects to modern life.

**Impact** – These books give clear examples of how nature and human choices are linked. Learning about peatlands shows us hidden places that protect our planet’s air. Understanding the new climate law reveals how governments can take big steps to slow global warming. Questioning old economic ideas helps us think about making fairer decisions for everyone.

**What's next step** – Readers can use these ideas to care more about the environment and support smart policies. Scientists and leaders may build on this knowledge to protect nature better and create laws that help fight climate change and improve society.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New books in 2026 highlight the power of nature’s hidden places and smart laws to shape a healthier planet and society.
articles.personality_title_fr: De nouveaux livres révèlent comment la nature et la politique façonnent notre avenir
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Des scientifiques et auteurs explorent des sujets importants comme l’environnement, le changement climatique et l’économie à travers de nouveaux livres publiés en 2026. Ces ouvrages nous aident à comprendre comment fonctionne la nature et comment les lois influencent notre monde.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Cinq livres remarquables ont été présentés, chacun offrant un regard unique. Le livre de Merritt Turetsky explique comment les tourbières, des zones humides spéciales, stockent beaucoup de carbone et aident à lutter contre le changement climatique. Leah Stokes raconte comment elle a contribué à faire adopter une grande loi américaine investissant plus de 400 milliards de dollars pour réduire le réchauffement climatique. James Galbraith remet en question les anciennes idées économiques et montre comment l’argent et le pouvoir influencent la politique aujourd’hui. Un autre livre de Timothy Baker explore comment la physique se lie à la vie moderne.

**Impact** – Ces livres donnent des exemples clairs de la façon dont la nature et les choix humains sont liés. Apprendre sur les tourbières nous montre des lieux cachés qui protègent l’air de notre planète. Comprendre la nouvelle loi sur le climat révèle comment les gouvernements peuvent agir fortement pour ralentir le réchauffement. Remettre en question les anciennes idées économiques aide à réfléchir à des décisions plus justes pour tous.

**Étape suivante** – Les lecteurs peuvent utiliser ces idées pour mieux protéger l’environnement et soutenir des politiques intelligentes. Les scientifiques et dirigeants pourront s’appuyer sur ces connaissances pour mieux préserver la nature et créer des lois aidant à lutter contre le changement climatique et améliorer la société.

**Une phrase clé** – Les nouveaux livres de 2026 montrent le rôle des lieux naturels cachés et des lois efficaces pour construire une planète et une société plus saines.

articles.title: Tribute to farmer who 'saved rare cattle breed'
articles.summary: Eric Freeman was a pioneering advocate for local rare breeds on his farm in Gloucestershire.
articles.content:
A bench has been unveiled in memory of a farmer and conservationist said to be instrumental in saving a rare breed of British cattle from extinction.

The bench in Newent, Gloucestershire, celebrates Eric Freeman, who promoted Gloucester cattle, Cotswold sheep and Gloucestershire Old Spot pigs on his farm in Taynton, and is credited with helping to revive wassailing in the county.

He died in 2023 aged 91, and his friend, cheese maker Charles Martell, remembered: "It would take Eric two hours to get from the library to the post office because he knew everybody and he didn't do short chats."

Freeman's granddaughter, Natasha James, said he would have been "thrilled" by the honour.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the conservation efforts of a farmer who played a key role in saving rare local livestock breeds from extinction, which has meaningful environmental and biodiversity impact. The tribute reflects recognition of his significant contribution to preserving agricultural heritage and rare species, benefiting broader society and environment.
articles.personality_title: Local farmer honored for saving rare British cattle breed
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Eric Freeman was a farmer and conservationist from Gloucestershire, England. He worked to protect rare local farm animals that were at risk of disappearing.

**What happened** – A bench was placed in Newent, Gloucestershire, to honor Eric Freeman after his death in 2023 at age 91. He was known for raising Gloucester cattle, Cotswold sheep, and Gloucestershire Old Spot pigs on his farm in Taynton. He also helped bring back the wassailing tradition in the area.

**Impact** – Freeman’s efforts helped save important rare farm animals from extinction. These animals are part of Britain’s farming history and local environment. By protecting them, he supported biodiversity and kept farming traditions alive.

**What’s next step** – The tribute bench allows the community to remember Freeman’s work. His example may encourage others to care for rare breeds and continue conservation efforts in farming.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Eric Freeman’s dedication preserved rare British farm animals and inspired ongoing conservation in Gloucestershire.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un agriculteur local honoré pour avoir sauvé une race bovine britannique rare
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un banc a été installé à Newent, Gloucestershire, pour rendre hommage à Eric Freeman après sa mort en 2023 à l’âge de 91 ans. Il était connu pour élever des bovins Gloucester, des moutons Cotswold et des cochons Gloucestershire Old Spot dans sa ferme à Taynton. Il a aussi aidé à relancer la tradition du wassailing dans la région.

**Impact** – Les efforts de Freeman ont aidé à sauver d’importants animaux de ferme rares de l’extinction. Ces animaux font partie de l’histoire agricole et de l’environnement local. En les protégeant, il a soutenu la biodiversité et maintenu les traditions agricoles.

**Prochaine étape** – Le banc commémoratif permet à la communauté de se souvenir du travail de Freeman. Son exemple peut encourager d’autres personnes à prendre soin des races rares et à poursuivre les efforts de conservation en agriculture.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le dévouement d’Eric Freeman a préservé des animaux de ferme rares britanniques et inspiré la conservation continue dans le Gloucestershire.
